name: Nikhil Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Nikhil. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group, not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and everything you say is confidential. That means you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Brennan's, a small builder, six of us and the boss. We do one or two houses at a time in the villages round here, detached places for people who've sold up in the city. I'm mostly on framing and roofs: stud walls, joists, rafters, getting it watertight before the weather turns. Start at half seven, flask of tea in the cab, and old Brennan comes by around ten to check we haven't cut anything backwards.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what's hard about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's the same job, done right, every time. A roof's a roof, and when the felt's on and the battens are straight you can go home and sleep. Hard part is it's not great money, Brennan's always paid a bit under, but there's not much else nearby, and Priya's on part-time at the supermarket. My knees have started complaining on the ladder too, which nobody warns you about at twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Most of these things get talked up and then you never hear about them again. I'm not on social media, so I'd just say it in the cab or at Priya's mum's on Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing changes, and that's fine. I don't use any of those AI programs, never have. The phone does calls and the football scores and that's enough for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Go to work, do the roofs, pay the mortgage. If Brennan wanted to try some computer thing for the paperwork, that's his business, not mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same as now, which is a bit tight but it's what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the money's tight. Would anything in this picture help with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. If anything, things cost the same and pay stays the same, like always. I'd keep an eye out for a better-paid firm, but there isn't one within forty minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you talk to about this kind of thing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not many people. My brother-in-law Sunil reads all the news and tells me what to worry about. I nod and then I go back to work.

S0.say: He's not surprised, because most new things get talked up and then disappear. He'd say it in the cab or at family Sunday lunch, not online.
S0.think: Nothing changes for him and that's fine; he has never used AI programs. His phone does calls and football scores, and that's enough.
S0.do: Carries on as normal: works, does the roofs and pays the mortgage. Leaves any computer paperwork tools to his boss.
S0.feel: Calm, because it's the tight but familiar life he knows.
S0.quote: The phone does calls and the football scores and that's enough for me.
S0.fieldNote: Nikhil is quiet, steady and set in his ways; he gives short answers and moves on. He doesn't blame anyone, just shrugs at hype. His brother-in-law Sunil is the one who brings the news into his life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's how things go, there's always something new. Some people will do well and some won't. I wouldn't make a big fuss about it at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think a small firm like Brennan's would be one of the last to change. He still writes the invoices by hand. The big housebuilders might go for robots and factory-made houses, but for us, I reckon I'd be all right for a good while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the same as now. I'd keep my head down and do good work so Brennan doesn't think about replacing me. If Priya wanted to put a bit aside each month I'd go along with it, but I wouldn't be signing up for any courses unless I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Maybe a little niggle at the back, but nothing I'd lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make that niggle grow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Brennan retired and sold up to one of the big firms. He's sixty-four and his son isn't interested. That's the bit I don't like thinking about, because then it's not my choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd avoid courses unless you had to. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not good at classrooms, never was. I'd sooner learn something by doing it, on site, with someone showing me. And at my age, with the kids and the mortgage, I don't fancy starting from the bottom.

S1.say: It's how things go: there's always something new, some do well and some don't. He wouldn't make a fuss at work.
S1.think: He believes a small firm like Brennan's, where invoices are still handwritten, would be among the last to change. Big housebuilders might move to robots and factory houses, but he expects to be fine for a good while.
S1.do: Keeps his head down and does good work so his boss has no reason to replace him. Goes along with saving a little each month if his partner wants, but avoids courses unless forced.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with a small niggle at the back of his mind.
S1.quote: He still writes the invoices by hand.
S1.fieldNote: His calm rests on his boss's old-fashioned habits, which may be a fragile shelter. The real threat he names is Brennan retiring and selling to a bigger firm, which he'd rather not think about. He prefers learning by doing, not classrooms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's terrible, and somebody needs to do something about it. I don't really know who, the government I suppose. But I'd say it quietly, I'm not one for marching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared. Two years and the robots can do roofs? I'm forty-three, I can't do anything else, and we've got less than a month's money. I wouldn't know where to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd tell Priya and we'd cut back hard: no takeaways, no new school shoes until they're actually worn through, cancel the sports channel. I'd ask Sunil if he knows any work going, anything, even warehouse, though I suppose robots would be there too. I'd keep turning up at Brennan's for as long as there's a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I can't breathe. Like when you miss a step on the ladder and there's nothing under your foot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't know where to start. If you had two years of warning, what would you do with them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the thing, I don't know. Everyone keeps saying 'learn new skills', but which? If the machines can do everything, what am I supposed to learn? I'd probably just keep working and hope it doesn't happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Arjun's thirteen, he'd probably know before I did, he's on that phone all day. I'd tell him we'd be all right, even if I didn't believe it. Meera's nine, I wouldn't tell her anything, I'd just let her be a kid.

S2.say: It's terrible and somebody, probably the government, needs to do something. He'd say it quietly, not at a march.
S2.think: He'd be scared: robots doing roofs in two years, no other skills at forty-three and under a month's savings. He wouldn't know where to start.
S2.do: Tells Priya and cuts back hard on takeaways, school shoes and the sports channel. Asks his brother-in-law about any work going, even warehouse jobs, and keeps turning up at Brennan's as long as there's work.
S2.feel: Panicked, like missing a step on the ladder with nothing under his foot.
S2.quote: Like when you miss a step on the ladder and there's nothing under your foot.
S2.fieldNote: His usual calm collapses completely here, which shows how much of it depended on things staying the same. He can't picture what he'd retrain for, so he falls back on hoping. He'd protect his younger child from the news altogether.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's better than two years, at least people can get ready. The government should help people like me who work with their hands. Maybe training, maybe some kind of money while you change over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I'd still be worried, just slower. Five years is time to notice it coming, but I'm not sure I'd know what to do with it. I'd keep hoping it wouldn't reach roofs in the villages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to save, even if it's twenty quid a week, so we're not at zero. I'd keep working and ask Brennan what he's thinking of doing. If someone told me exactly which course to do, I might do it, but I wouldn't go looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Not the panic of the fast one, but I'd be thinking about it on every ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have time to get a bit of money aside and maybe see what other people are doing. With two years, it's just a punch. With five, it's more like watching a storm come in, and you've got time to get the washing off the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you go to for advice on what to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sunil, probably, he works in an office for the council. Or Brennan, who's seen a few ups and downs. I wouldn't trust anything on the internet.

S3.say: Five years is better than two because people can get ready, and the government should help manual workers with training or income while they change over.
S3.think: He'd still be worried, just more slowly: five years is time to notice it coming, but he isn't sure what to do with it. He'd hope it never reaches roofs in the villages.
S3.do: Saves even twenty a week so the family isn't at zero and asks his boss what he plans to do. Would take a course only if someone told him exactly which one.
S3.feel: Alarmed, thinking about it on every ladder, though without the panic of the fast version.
S3.quote: With five, it's more like watching a storm come in, and you've got time to get the washing off the line.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time helps him a little, mainly by letting him save, but he still waits for someone else to point the way. He trusts family and his boss, not the internet. His imagery is domestic and everyday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, plenty can happen. People will work it out. I'd tell the lads not to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years feels less scary. I'd be fifty-three, the mortgage would be a lot smaller, and Arjun and Meera would be grown or nearly. Brennan would probably have retired by then anyway, so I'd be looking for something new regardless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, save a bit more, maybe pay a little extra off the mortgage when there's overtime. If I saw a few other roofers going off and learning something that worked, I'd think about following them. I'd want to see it working first though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more of a slow worry. Ten years gives me time to get used to the idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd follow others if it worked for them. What would 'working' look like to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone like me, same age, same kind of job, who's moved over and is paying their bills. Not some young lad, not someone with a degree. If I saw that, I'd ask him how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said a small firm would be slow to change. Do you still think that with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough for even Brennan to change, or to sell up. So no, not really. I'd still be among the last, which is something.

S4.say: Ten years is a long time and people will work it out. He'd tell his workmates not to panic.
S4.think: Ten years feels less scary: at fifty-three the mortgage would be smaller, the children grown or nearly, and his boss likely retired, so he'd be looking for new work anyway.
S4.do: Keeps working, saves a bit more and pays extra off the mortgage with overtime. Waits to see someone his own age and trade move over successfully before following.
S4.feel: Anxious in a slow way, with time to get used to the idea.
S4.quote: Someone like me, same age, same kind of job, who's moved over and is paying their bills.
S4.fieldNote: Nikhil needs a role model who looks exactly like him before he'll move. Ten years softens the fear because his family's stakes fall as the mortgage shrinks and the children grow. He drops his earlier belief that a small firm would shelter him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd have no money saved and no idea what else to do, and I don't think anyone would help in time. What would help is somebody showing me, plainly, what work there is and teaching me on the job, with enough pay to keep the house while I learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe you should have asked about the knees. Even without robots, I don't know how many more winters I've got on a roof. Funny thing is, the robots might come just about when my body gives out anyway.

headlineQuote: Funny thing is, the robots might come just about when my body gives out anyway.
portrait: Nikhil Abbott is a 43-year-old framer and roofer at a small village builder, quiet and steady, who has never used an AI program and doesn't want to. He feels calm in AI Plateau and Steady Disruption, trusting that his old-fashioned boss would be the last to change. AGI by 2028 leaves him panicked and without a plan, cutting back and asking family about any work. With five or ten years he saves a little and waits to see someone just like him make the move first. He blames no one in particular and looks to family, his boss and, vaguely, the government.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd have no savings, no idea what else to do and no help in time.
whatWouldHelp: Someone plainly showing him what work exists and teaching him on the job, with enough pay to keep the house while he learns.
